EcheniqueThe problem
02 / 14

An open-source, column-oriented database built for analytics

Columnar

Stores each column separately and compressed, so a query reads only the columns it needs.

Analytical (OLAP)

Made for counting, summing and grouping huge tables, with data inserted in batches.

Queried with SQL

Familiar language, but no transactions and updates are expensive: it is not a classic relational database.

Is it NoSQL?

It belongs to the column-store family: a non-relational storage model that still speaks SQL. Created at Yandex, open source since 2016.

EcheniqueWhat is ClickHouse
03 / 14

To sum amounts by status, read 2 columns, not 5

Row store: reads every whole row

id · restaurant · status · amount · time
id · restaurant · status · amount · time
id · restaurant · status · amount · time

5 of 5 columns read

Column store: reads only what it needs

id
rest.
status
amount
time

2 of 5 columns read, the rest skipped

Sorted by a key

MergeTree keeps rows ordered, so a query skips blocks that cannot match.

Merged in the background

Each insert writes a new part; ClickHouse merges parts later.

Heavily compressed

14 million real Criteo rows take only 262 MiB on disk.

05 / 14

One ClickHouse, three kinds of data, never mixed

Simulated customers

Fictional

A traffic simulator with rules and a fixed seed. Hundreds of customers search, compare, buy or give up.

AI agents

Fictional

A small local language model (Ollama, qwen3:0.6b) decides each step and explains why. Python validates it.

Downloaded datasets

Real, public

Criteo advertising experiment (14.0 M rows) and the Glovo product catalog (2.9 M products).

Each row keeps its origin, so a number from the simulation is never presented as real data, and real datasets are never joined with fictional orders.

Status and next steps before 15 November

Done

  • Full path working: app → API → ClickHouse → dashboard
  • Three data views, with real datasets loaded and verified
  • Public read-only website
  • Automated tests and installation guide

Next

  • Final talk centred on ClickHouse
  • Two new dashboards: Customer Journey and ClickHouse Performance
  • Insert, update and delete shown live
  • Install test on another computer

Limits we found

  • Updates and deletes are expensive, so we only insert
  • Duplicates collapse later, in background merges
  • One node: replication explained, not deployed
  • Long runs: Docker closed twice on the demo PC

The answer is the same. The amount of work changes.

GPS history

courier_positions → argMax()

Compute the latest state from the history on every request.

Prepared latest state

courier_latest_state → argMaxMerge()

Merge the states maintained by the materialized view.

Reported server metricHistoryPrepared state
Median rows read per query4,371,336150
Median server time · 1 reader560–562 ms6 ms
Peak memory per query8.02 MiB4.03 MiB

The read becomes cheaper. Maintaining the view also costs work during ingestion; that cost is a separate experiment.
